subject: English
topic: Advanced Tense Usage — Complex Structures (W11 B1)

questions.stem:
Choose the correct tense form:
'By the time you ___ home, I ___ the dinner.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'By the time' introduces a time clause that refers to a future point — time clauses with 'by the time' use Present Simple (not Future) for the subordinate clause. The main clause uses Future Perfect to show an action will be completed before that future time. 'By the time you REACH home, I WILL HAVE COOKED dinner.' Trap: 'will reach' is wrong in a time clause (Simple Present replaces Future in time clauses); 'will cook' = simple future (doesn't show completion before the time reference).

questions.stem:
Choose the correct form:
'She ___ in this company for ten years when she finally ___ a promotion.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Had been working' = Past Perfect Continuous, used for an action that was ongoing up to a past point ('finally got a promotion' = past event). The continuous form emphasises the duration (ten years of working). 'When she finally got' = simple past for the completed event. Trap: 'has worked' = Present Perfect (wrong tense — 'finally got' is past); 'was working' = Past Continuous (doesn't emphasise the duration relative to the past event as strongly as Past Perfect Continuous).

questions.stem:
Identify the correct sentence:
(A) If it will rain, we will cancel the match.
(B) If it rains, we will cancel the match.
(C) If it rained, we will cancel the match.
(D) If it would rain, we would cancel the match.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Real/likely future condition: If + Simple Present, will + infinitive. 'If it RAINS, we WILL cancel the match.' Trap: A uses 'will rain' in the if-clause — future tense is NOT used in conditional 'if' clauses; C uses 'rained' — past simple (this would be hypothetical: 'If it rained, we would cancel'); D uses 'would rain' — doubly wrong as both clauses use 'would' (hypothetical form mixes type 2 if-clause incorrectly).

questions.stem:
Fill in the blank with the correct verb form:
'I wish I ___ more time to prepare for the examination.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'I wish' + past simple (or 'were') is used to express a wish about the PRESENT that is contrary to fact. 'I wish I HAD more time' = I don't have enough time now (present reality). Compare: 'I wish I HAD STUDIED harder' = past regret (wish + past perfect). Trap: 'have' = present tense (cannot follow 'wish' in standard grammar for hypothetical wishes); 'would have' = used in wish sentences about future habits ('I wish you would stop that'), not present situations.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct form:
'The report ___ by the time the manager arrives tomorrow morning.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'By the time + future reference' → Future Perfect (Active: will have prepared) or Future Perfect Passive (will have been prepared). The subject is 'the report' (passive, since reports don't prepare themselves). 'The report WILL HAVE BEEN PREPARED by the time the manager arrives.' This is Future Perfect Passive. Trap: 'will be prepared' = simple future passive (doesn't show completion before the reference time); 'has been prepared' = Present Perfect (wrong tense for future reference); 'will prepare' is active and wrong for 'the report' as subject.

questions.stem:
Identify the correct sentence about a hypothetical past situation:
(A) If I had studied harder, I would pass the exam.
(B) If I studied harder, I would have passed the exam.
(C) If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam.
(D) If I would have studied, I would pass the exam.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Type 3 conditional (hypothetical past — imagining the past was different): If + Past Perfect, would + have + past participle. 'If I HAD STUDIED harder, I WOULD HAVE PASSED the exam.' Both clauses correctly use the Type 3 form. Trap: A = mixed type (past perfect in if-clause but present 'would pass' in main = Type 2/3 mix, wrong); B = Type 2 if-clause with Type 3 main (inconsistent); D = 'would have studied' in if-clause — 'would' is never used in the if-clause.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct form:
'He ___ in this house since his birth.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Since his birth' = a specific starting point in the past continuing to now. Present Perfect (HAS LIVED) is used for an action that started in the past and still continues. 'He HAS LIVED in this house since his birth' = he started living there at birth and still does. Trap: 'lived' = simple past (implies he no longer lives there); 'had lived' = Past Perfect (needs another past event to be completed before); 'lives' = present simple (misses the 'since birth' duration aspect).

questions.stem:
Choose the correct tense:
'When we arrived at the station, the train ___ already.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. When two past events happen in sequence, the earlier event uses Past Perfect and the later uses Simple Past. The train leaving = earlier event (Past Perfect: HAD DEPARTED). Arriving at the station = later event (Simple Past: arrived). 'When we ARRIVED, the train HAD ALREADY DEPARTED.' The word 'already' reinforces that the departure preceded the arrival. Trap: 'departed' = simple past (grammatically possible but doesn't clearly show sequence); 'was departing' = continuous (the train was in the process of departing when we arrived — different meaning); 'has departed' = Present Perfect (wrong tense for a past-sequence event).

questions.stem:
Choose the correct sentence:
'The scientists ___ on this project for five years before they finally published their findings.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Before they finally published' = a completed past event. The five-year working period was ongoing UP TO that past publication point. Past Perfect Continuous (HAD BEEN WORKING) = duration + continuity up to a past reference point. 'They HAD BEEN WORKING for five years before they published.' Trap: 'were working' = Past Continuous (doesn't convey the duration aspect as powerfully, and doesn't link the five years to the publication event); 'have been working' = Present Perfect Continuous (wrong — the publication is in the past).

questions.stem:
Spot the tense error:
'Yesterday, while she was cooking dinner, her phone rings and she burnt her hand.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Yesterday' signals the entire sentence is in the past. 'Was cooking' = Past Continuous (correct for background action). 'Rings' = Present Simple — WRONG. It should be 'RANG' (Simple Past) to match the past-time context. 'Burnt' = Simple Past (correct for the sudden result). Corrected: 'Yesterday, while she was cooking dinner, her phone RANG and she burnt her hand.' Trap: 'was cooking' is correct (past continuous for ongoing action interrupted by a simple past event); 'burnt' is correct past simple; 'has burnt' would be wrong (Present Perfect doesn't match 'yesterday').
